paragraphs: He said: the reason that drove our opponents to the doctrine of opinion and analogy is that they found things that one needs to know — whether they are permitted or forbidden — that are not explicitly written in the Torah, and likewise quantities and modalities that are not articulated [in Scripture]. They knew, at the same time, that it is impermissible to say of the Maker (mighty and exalted) that He left mankind in a state of bewilderment; rather there must inevitably be something He set in place to guide them to His intended meaning in these matters. And they knew, at the same time, that if they kept silent on this point and refrained from claiming that qiyās is the indicator God set up to lead His servants to what is not explicit in Scripture, they would soon be forced to acknowledge the Mishnah and Talmud, in which all of these matters are explicated. So they jumped to the doctrine of qiyās as a defensive maneuver — to ward off the consequence that would otherwise force them to acknowledge the āthār (oral-traditional reports). They said: "Qiyās suffices us, and there are no oral-traditional reports transmitted from the Prophet."

He said: let us begin with what they have used in support of establishing qiyās in the report-based commandments, then expose its corruption. He said: as for Anan, he argued for the establishment of qiyās by saying that the two tablets were inscribed on both sides.[{3}] He said: as for Benjamin [al-Nahawandī], he argued for it by the words of the Prophet (Prov 2:4–5): "Seek her as silver, and search her as hidden treasure — then shalt thou understand the powers of God…". He said: Anan also mentioned this. And [Benjamin] held that this searching (taftīsh) that the Prophet commanded after wisdom is the establishment of the laws of the Torah by what naẓar obligates. He said: but this is null and void; for taftīsh (searching) in the [Hebrew] tongue does not designate the bringing into being of a [new] law, but rather designates the quest of the searcher for something already existing[{4}] — as Scripture says of the cup (Gen 44:12): "And he searched, beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest" — where the cup exists. And likewise (Gen 31:35): "And he searched but did not find the idols." And likewise (1 Sam 23:23): "I will search for him among all the thousands of Judah." He said: but as for a "searching" that aims at the bringing forth of what does not exist — that is not in the [Hebrew] tongue. He said: even if we conceded to them that taftīsh could mean the bringing-forth of what is non-existent, [the seeker] would only be looking for [something already existing]; and the silver and the hidden treasure to which wisdom is compared — the seeker who seeks them aims at the acquisition of their physical instances, not at the generation of new instances.

He said: some of the latter-day [Karaites] argue for the obligation of qiyās from the saying of God (Deut 22:26): "And the matter of this one [the betrothed maiden raped in the field] is like one who rises up against his neighbor and slays him." They say: just as Scripture here compares the rapist of the betrothed maiden to the murderer, so we likewise are obligated to compare one thing to another that resembles it. He said: but ask them, first: tell us about this biblical pericope[{5}] that you have made into an instance of analogy: did the Eternal do this because it was obligatory upon Him to make an analogy, or because it was not obligatory upon Him? If they say "because it was obligatory," they have thereby claimed that the Eternal (mighty and exalted) cannot initiate a precept for His servants except by way of a previous analogue. This entails — among other absurdities — that the Eternal cannot initiate a precept as such on His servants but only as built on something prior; that His precept must be analogically grounded on a precept of His prior; and accordingly that His acts are analogically grounded on prior acts — yielding an infinite regress. They thereby cancel the very origination of things by claiming an unending chain of mutual analogies. The same regress entails that the precept itself is qadīm without limit, and that since the precept presupposes a community to receive it, the eternity of creation alongside God is established. If they say "no, it was not obligatory upon Him," they have thereby conceded that qiyās is not obligatory — and Deut 22:26 is then merely an initial precept from the Maker that happened to coincide with the form of analogy.[{6}]

He said: it can also be said to them: qiyās, on your own definition, takes effect only when there is an agreement (wifāq) between the two compared items in some respect or respects — and some of you say "in a respect." So tell us: in what respects does murder agree with fornication? You know perfectly well that murder cannot be made permissible by money and witnesses, whereas fornication can be made permissible by money and witnesses (i.e., bride-price and marriage-contract witnesses). Murder is not, ordinarily, consented to between killer and killed, whereas fornication can be agreed between a man and a woman who arrange to lie together. So since there is no antecedent agreement between the two — there is no qiyās here. Where is the wifāq that would underwrite the analogy? Of further dissimilarities: the murderer's penalty is "like for like" (life for life), but the adulterer's penalty is not "like for like." The unintentional killer is jailed, but the unintentional adulterer is not. So this whole argument that Deut 22:26 was a qiyās fails — it is no analogy at all, but a fresh initiation by God.

He further claims that the phrase "like one who rises up" is not a categorical (ḥatm) statement but a possibility (imkān) one. For it could be the contrary: the lawgiver could have said, "do not kill this maiden, since perhaps she cried out and was not heeded" — so that the meaning of [Deut 22:27], "she cried out," is implicit in the form "it is possible that she cried out." God says to His servants: you do not know; and since it might be that she was forcibly violated, do not kill her, leave her alone — for that does not escape Me. He said: this is a clear sense of the passage. He said: even if we conceded to them that Scripture itself performed a qiyās, that would not license us to perform qiyās — just as Scripture initiated legislation, but that does not license us to initiate legislation.

He said: some of the latter-day [Karaites] argue: "we have observed that a first person is alive, sensing, mobile — and we have inferred from this that he is originated; and we are thereby obligated to make the same judgment about every person. By analogy, then, when we know a ruling in the law for one thing, we must make the same ruling for everything that resembles it." He said: but this analogy is manifestly broken. We did not judge the second person to be originated by analogy with the first — rather, even if the first had never existed at all, and we had only ever seen the second, we would have judged him individually to be originated, since the very same evidence that indicated origination in the first is present in the second.[{7}] He said: but in the legal sphere, were we not to know the ruling of the first matter, we would have no route to obligate the same ruling on its analogue. The asymmetry is irrecoverable.

He said: the relation of the rational farāʾiḍ (those known by reason) to the report-based ones in this matter is like the relation of rational propositions to report-based propositions: the one set generalizes, the other does not. If we have rationally established that "man is a speaking mortal," it is obligatory that every man be such — since we did not predicate this of any particular individual. But if we know by report that some particular man is literate and skilled in calculation, it does not follow that every man is. So too in law: if theft is intrinsically reprehensible by reason, every theft is reprehensible — for any one instance is the analogue of any other. But if what report prohibits is some particular item, then that item is what is prohibited — and others cannot be brought under it by qiyās.

He said: how, then, can qiyās be valid in the report-based laws — when those laws are not themselves built on qiyās? If the roots (uṣūl) are not so constituted, it is impermissible for the branches (furūʿ) to be so constituted, since otherwise the branches contradict the roots. The one who reasons by analogy intends to bring his ruling into agreement with the principle, not into contradiction with it — so if he posits the furūʿ as analogically built while the uṣūl are not, he has contradicted the principle in the very act of trying to harmonize with it. He said: now let us show how the laws of the Torah are not set on analogical foundations. The forms of qiyās are three: (i) the qiyās of the logicians (qiyās al-manṭiqiyyīn), (ii) the qiyās of the dialecticians (qiyās al-jadaliyyīn), and (iii) the qiyās of the people of our own religion (qiyās ahl dīnnā).[{8}] He said: when one examines the laws of the Torah, one finds that the demonstration is to be taken from the four kinds of cause — material, formal, efficient, and final — as articulated in the books of logic.

If we apply these four causes to our laws, we find their rulings to contradict them. Material cause: The material cause of the permission to eat the flesh of cattle is its being "cloven-hoofed and chewing the cud" (Lev 11:3). But we find many cloven-hoofed and cud-chewing animals whose flesh is prohibited to eat — because they are carrion, or torn, or sanctified [for sacrifice], or the like. The material cause is present, but the ruling is suspended.[{9}] Formal cause: A leper is impure on account of the white discoloration in his flesh. But we find him pure when the discoloration has spread over his entire body (cf. Lev 13:13).[{10}] The formal cause is present, but the ruling is reversed. Efficient cause: The priest is licensed to eat the minḥa (meal-offering) on account of his offering it. But we find him offering a minḥa and yet not licensed to eat it — as Scripture says (Lev 6:16): "And every meal-offering of the priest shall be wholly burnt; it shall not be eaten." Final cause: The final cause of the altar is to receive sacrifices and peace-offerings. But we find an altar built and ready, yet sacrifice and peace-offering forbidden on it — namely on the Sabbath and on the Day of Atonement. If any of these four causes were genuinely operative in the farāʾiḍ, no exception to it would obtain — as we have shown. He said: if anyone tries to escape by saying that these exceptions do not cancel the causes but are merely restrictions on them — we reply: precisely because they are restricted by exceptions and conditions, they cease to be true causes-and-principles in the report-based commandment.

He said: as for qiyās of the dialecticians — which is the application of the cause in its effect — this kind too fails in the laws of the Torah. For it makes the cause of protecting human blood that man is "in the noble image" (Gen 9:6) — yet it then licenses the blood of the disbeliever and of the betrothed-violator, whose human form is the same noble image. The same disparities appear elsewhere: one who strikes his slave who then dies after two days is not punished (Exod 21:21), "for he is his property"; but one whose slave dies at his hand (Exod 21:20) is punished — even though "his property" is the same relation in both cases, and the relation holds at the same first instant. The granddaughter is prohibited because she is "your nakedness" (Lev 18:10); but the wife — who is equally "your nakedness" (Lev 18:8: "thy father's wife is thy father's nakedness, uncover not her nakedness") — is permitted to her own husband. And the maternal uncle's wife is forbidden as "your relative's nakedness" (Lev 20:19–20), but the female cousin and other female relatives in the same degree are permitted — even though all are equally "of one's kin," as Scripture explicitly says (Lev 25:49): "or any near relative of his flesh."[{11}]

He said: as for the qiyās of the people of our religion and of other legalists, that consists in equating two equals, distinguishing two distincts, and judging the greater by the lesser. These three operations of qiyās also contradict the Torah's rulings. The Torah distinguishes two equals: It differentiates between the ox-thief and the sheep-thief and their slaughterers (Exod 21:37) — making one pay four, the other five — though both are equally livestock. It equates the garment-thief and the donkey-thief — both pay two-fold — though the garment is inanimate and the donkey is alive (Exod 22:3). It equates the eye and the tooth of a slave (Exod 21:26–27) — making the master free the slave for either injury — though reason easily distinguishes their relative gravity. It differentiates the killer of a free man and the killer of a slave (Exod 21:20–23) — though reason equalizes them since the killer is no more master of the slave's life than of the free man's. It binds the unintentional homicide to imprisonment (in the city of refuge) but not to a sacrificial offering — whereas it binds every other unintentional offender to a sacrificial offering but not to imprisonment. It permits postponement [of certain fasts] by a fast-day but not by a festival or Sabbath. It obligates qaḍāʾ (making up) of the Pesach if missed (Num 9:10–11), but obligates no qaḍāʾ for the rest of the festivals. The ascetic[{12}] who eats meat to excess is not in violation; if he eats so much as a single grape, he is in violation. The reverse holds for ordinary people. And in ʿarakhin (vow-valuations: Lev 27), it values the 19-year-old at fifty silver shekels and the 20-year-old equally at fifty — but values the 21-year-old as the equivalent of the 59-year-old. And it equates the eighty-year-old female with the sixteen-year-old female at eighteen silver shekels. It values the slave worth fifty drachma and the slave worth one thousand denarii equally at thirty silver shekels (Exod 21:32). It values the saline field and the most fertile field as equal at fifty silver shekels (Lev 27:16ff.). And so on — the list is endless. The point is that the laws equate what qiyās would distinguish, and distinguish what qiyās would equate.

He said: how then can anyone claim the operation of logical qiyās in the Torah's commandments when he sees this — especially in the laws governing men and women, which differ as starkly as possible? A man may marry two women, but a woman may not marry two men. A man may divorce his wife, but a woman may not divorce her husband. A man's divorcée is forbidden to him after she has been to another, but the inverse disability cannot be imposed — since a woman cannot divorce in the first place. The male priest officiates but the female priest does not. The male priest eats of the qodesh ha-qodashim but the female priest does not. The male priest may not marry a divorcée but the female may marry one previously divorced. The man is obligated to pilgrimage three times a year but the woman is not. The father may annul his daughter's vows but no one may annul a son's vows. The son receives a greater share in inheritance than the daughter, and only the firstborn son is the bekhor who takes a double portion.[{13}] He said: of such cases there are very many, all of which invalidate qiyās in the report-based commandments and the forbidden-degrees laws.

In sum, the whole of his discourse on this matter resolves into what Yaʿqūb b. Efraim al-Shāmī had argued: the commandments are of two kinds — rational (ʿaqliyya) and report-based (samʿiyya). The rational ones — like the prohibition of murder, of fornication, of theft, and the like — are such that even had revelation not delivered them, reason would have obligated their prohibition. The report-based ones — like the Sabbath, Pesach, the fringes of garments, circumcision, and the like — have no cause-in-reason at all; we know them by samʿ alone. He said: in the first category of commandments qiyās is licit because they are built on reason and therefore stand together with what qiyās yields. In the second category — which is samʿī — qiyās is not licit, because they have no cause-in-reason to which qiyās can be built. Al-Fayyūmī himself — though he did not present the argument in this form — gives a position whose force entails al-Shāmī's doctrine; he in fact spells this out in a passage where he says: "the rational and the report-based commandments are like the rational and the report-based propositions, of which one cannot be analogically reasoned to the other." Thus he has explicitly affirmed that qiyās applies to the rational commandments and does not apply to the report-based ones.[{15}] ---
